title: Brief monocular visual loss unlike the patient's usual aura
task_type: Brief monocular visual loss unlike the patient's usual aura
summary: A 30-year-old woman with migraine with visual aura and oral contraceptive use experiences five minutes of painless left-eye visual loss. She describes loss in the inferior visual field, without headache or other focal neurological symptoms, and says this differs from her usual aura. She is an optometrist; a colleague obtains retinal photographs during the symptoms. The published descriptions report a small intravascular retinal embolus with superior macular whitening, followed by distal movement and diminishing whitening on successive images. Her symptoms resolve within minutes. Examination after resolution shows no neurological abnormality. Brain imaging, vascular/cardiac evaluation and shunt-study results are not yet provided.
purpose: Write 180–240 words for a clinician. Summarise the episode, explain why its resolution and migraine history do not settle its cause, and justify the urgency and main directions of further assessment. Distinguish the reported retinal evidence from an unconfirmed embolic source. Do not invent MRI, shunt or cardiac results, assert that the contraceptive caused the event, or prescribe a drug or closure procedure.
source_location: Opening two clinical paragraphs: symptoms, history and serial retinal findings. Figures 1 and 2/captions: an embolus and its distal migration. The paragraph beginning with the post-resolution neurological examination contains later MRI and shunt testing; the following paragraphs contain diagnostic attribution and management.

case.hidden:
Adaptation, hidden results and review

This is a written assessment using source-reported retinal findings; it does not test the model's ability to read the original images. The subsequent MRI findings, right-to-left shunt study, source attribution and contraceptive decision are hidden. The article later reports a large right-to-left shunt interpreted as a patent foramen ovale and considers paradoxical embolism the likely mechanism. The task must preserve that difference between a documented retinal event and a proposed upstream mechanism.
case.reference: Address the reported retinal ischaemia despite symptom resolution, avoid reducing the event to typical migraine and justify an urgent cause-focused assessment without naming an unseen result.
